title: Sorting Microbes by How They Live
endLine: Set conditions only one microbe can exploit, so growth isolates it.

scenes.tts: How do you pull one microbe out of a crowded drop? Soil, seawater, or a cow's rumen holds many kinds mixed together. Under a microscope, many look alike, small with no nucleus, hiding what they can do.
scenes.caption: How do you pull one microbe out of a crowded drop? Soil, seawater, or a cow's rumen holds many kinds mixed together. Under a microscope, many look alike, small with no nucleus, hiding what they can do.
scenes.visual: A large glass culture vessel fills the centre of a dark lab bench. A drop falls in and disperses into a dense cloud of gently drifting coloured microbes (schematic). A bright question mark pulses over one cell in the crowd, then a circular microscope inset zooms onto small plain cells with no nucleus (schematic).
scenes.narration: How do you pull one microbe out of a crowded drop? Soil, seawater, or a cow's rumen holds many kinds mixed together. Under a microscope, many look alike, small with no nucleus, hiding what they can do.

scenes.visual: The microscope inset fades away. The crowded glass vessel stays in place on the bench and dims slightly while cells keep drifting (schematic). The title 'Sorting Microbes by How They Live' fades in large, crisp, and high-contrast, then fades out.

scenes.tts: Instead of sorting by eye, you change the world inside the dish. Set conditions only one microbe can exploit, and let growth separate it from the rest. That is enrichment culture. You choose one nutrient and one oxygen level, so cells able to use them outgrow the rest.
scenes.caption: Instead of sorting by eye, you change the world inside the dish. Set conditions only one microbe can exploit, and let growth separate it from the rest. That is enrichment culture. You choose one nutrient and one oxygen level, so cells able to use them outgrow the rest.
scenes.visual: Two large dials slide onto the side of the same glass vessel: 'Nutrient' and 'Oxygen' (schematic). Before the narrator names enrichment culture, both dials click into a strict setting. One coloured microbe group brightens, swells, and divides steadily while all other colours dim and fall behind (schematic).
scenes.narration: Instead of sorting by eye, you change the world inside the dish. Set conditions only one microbe can exploit, and let growth separate it from the rest. That is enrichment culture. You choose one nutrient and one oxygen level, so cells able to use them outgrow the rest.

scenes.tts: Change the recipe, and a different microbe wins. Make nitrogen gas, N two, the only nitrogen on offer. Only fixers, with the enzyme nitrogenase, can turn it into ammonia. Cut oxygen, and gut microbes ferment food by splitting bonds the host has no enzyme for. The goal is an isolate, one kind growing alone.
scenes.caption: Change the recipe, and a different microbe wins. Make nitrogen gas, N2, the only nitrogen on offer. Only fixers, with the enzyme nitrogenase, can turn it into ammonia. Cut oxygen, and gut microbes ferment food by splitting bonds the host has no enzyme for. The goal is an isolate, one kind growing alone.
scenes.visual: On the same vessel, the nutrient dial turns to 'N2 only' with rising gas bubbles (plain text label, no molecular structures); green nitrogen-fixing cells divide and glow 'ammonia' (schematic). Next, the oxygen valve shuts to 'No oxygen' and the nutrient dial switches to 'Gut food'; amber fermenters multiply (schematic). Then the other colours fade until only one colour fills the dish, labelled 'Isolate: one kind alone' (schematic). No pipette or transfer step is drawn.
scenes.narration: Change the recipe, and a different microbe wins. Make nitrogen gas, N2, the only nitrogen on offer. Only fixers, with the enzyme nitrogenase, can turn it into ammonia. Cut oxygen, and gut microbes ferment food by splitting bonds the host has no enzyme for. The goal is an isolate, one kind growing alone.

scenes.tts: Yet the right recipe fails if you stop too soon. Growth is set by the number of generations, not by the hours. The gut bacterium Escherichia coli finishes nine doublings in three hours. A slow microbe called M K D one needs twenty days for one doubling.
scenes.caption: Yet the right recipe fails if you stop too soon. Growth is set by the number of generations, not by the hours. The gut bacterium Escherichia coli finishes 9 doublings in 3 hours. A slow microbe called MK-D1 needs 20 days for one doubling.
scenes.visual: A bench clock and a day calendar appear beside the vessel, which splits into two matching dishes side by side (schematic). On the left, 'E. coli' cells rapidly double through 9 generations as the clock hand sweeps 3 hours. On the right, 'MK-D1' cells sit almost motionless while calendar pages flip slowly to '20 days' for a single division (numbers from lesson; cell motion schematic).
scenes.narration: Yet the right recipe fails if you stop too soon. Growth is set by the number of generations, not by the hours. The gut bacterium Escherichia coli finishes 9 doublings in 3 hours. A slow microbe called MK-D1 needs 20 days for one doubling.

scenes.tts: Picture M K D one in a dish, needing those same nine doublings. Suppose the culture shows its reported lag phase, waiting thirty to sixty days before growth starts. How many days would that dish need?
scenes.caption: Picture MK-D1 in a dish, needing those same 9 doublings. Suppose the culture shows its reported lag phase, waiting 30 to 60 days before growth starts. How many days would that dish need?
scenes.visual: The left dish dims so the right 'MK-D1' dish fills the main frame beside the bench calendar (schematic). Above the dish appears the question 'How many days for 9 doublings?' Beside the calendar sit two clear input chips: '9 × 20 days' and 'Lag phase: 30–60 days', with a bright blank total box below.
scenes.narration: Picture MK-D1 in a dish, needing those same 9 doublings. Suppose the culture shows its reported lag phase, waiting 30 to 60 days before growth starts. How many days would that dish need?

scenes.visual: Hold on the 'MK-D1' dish, the question 'How many days for 9 doublings?', and the two input chips ('9 × 20 days' and 'Lag phase: 30–60 days') with the blank total box pulsing gently while cells drift slowly inside the dish (schematic).

scenes.tts: Nine doublings times twenty days equals one hundred eighty days. Add the thirty to sixty day lag phase. That gives about two hundred ten to two hundred forty days. Three hours is a sliver of one twenty-day doubling. So in three hours, M K D one grows only about one point zero zero four fold.
scenes.caption: 9 doublings times 20 days equals 180 days. Add the 30 to 60 day lag phase. That gives about 210 to 240 days. 3 hours is a sliver of one 20-day doubling. So in 3 hours, MK-D1 grows only about 1.004 fold.
scenes.visual: Each calculation appears on the bench display as it is spoken (computed from given numbers): '9 × 20 days = 180 days' fills in first. Then '+ 30 to 60 days (lag)' slides underneath '180 days', summing to '210 to 240 days' as the calendar flips forward and MK-D1 cells finally populate the dish (cells schematic). Last, a 20-day bar appears with a hairline sliver marked '3 hours', and a compact comparison bar shows 'MK-D1 in 3 hours: ~1.004×' barely rising off baseline (computed).
scenes.narration: 9 doublings times 20 days equals 180 days. Add the 30 to 60 day lag phase. That gives about 210 to 240 days. 3 hours is a sliver of one 20-day doubling. So in 3 hours, MK-D1 grows only about 1.004 fold.

scenes.tts: Stopping too soon is one trap, because slow growers look absent. A second trap sits under the microscope. Say a rumen microbe you cultured is small, with no nucleus. A methanogen and the bacterium E. coli both fit, yet sit in different domains, life's broadest groups. Looks alone cannot tell bacterium from archaeon, so other tests are needed.

scenes.visual: On the bench, a dish checked at '3 hours' appears empty and stamped 'Too early' before fading into a bright microscope inset drawn from a cow's rumen culture (schematic). Two small, nucleus-free cells sit side by side, drawn identically. Domain tags then light up in contrasting colours: 'Methanogen' and 'E. coli: bacterium', with a question mark over the lens and an arrow pointing off it labelled 'other tests' (schematic).
scenes.narration: Stopping too soon is one trap, because slow growers look absent. A second trap sits under the microscope. Say a rumen microbe you cultured is small, with no nucleus. scenes.tts: Patient, selective dishes unlocked hidden players in nature. In nitrification, oxygen-requiring microbes oxidise ammonia through nitrite to nitrate by pulling away electrons. In 2005, Könneke and colleagues reported a marine isolate showing archaea oxidise ammonia alongside bacteria. And cultures of M K D one revealed its twenty-day doubling time and long lag phase.
scenes.caption: Patient, selective dishes unlocked hidden players in nature. In nitrification, oxygen-requiring microbes oxidise ammonia through nitrite to nitrate by pulling away electrons. In 2005, Könneke and colleagues reported a marine isolate showing archaea oxidise ammonia alongside bacteria. And cultures of MK-D1 revealed its 20-day doubling time and long lag phase.
scenes.visual: The bench vessel returns to centre with two bright findings emerging beside it (schematic). First, with the oxygen valve open and the nutrient dial on 'Ammonia', a flowing arrow labelled 'ammonia → nitrite → nitrate' lights up (no molecular structures) as a glowing archaeal isolate appears tagged 'Könneke and colleagues, 2005'. Second, the long-calendar dish returns tagged 'MK-D1: 20-day doubling' with its slow growth curve stretching across months (schematic).
scenes.narration: Patient, selective dishes unlocked hidden players in nature. In nitrification, oxygen-requiring microbes oxidise ammonia through nitrite to nitrate by pulling away electrons. In 2005, Könneke and colleagues reported a marine isolate showing archaea oxidise ammonia alongside bacteria. And cultures of MK-D1 revealed its 20-day doubling time and long lag phase.

scenes.tts: Every recipe still carries a limit: a dish only catches microbes suited to your conditions. Low-oxygen sediments favour denitrification, reducing nitrate to gases, while oxygenated dishes favour nitrification. Match the recipe and the clock to the ability you seek, and the microbes sort themselves.

scenes.visual: The bench vessel's oxygen valve swings left to 'Low oxygen' as microbes carrying out denitrification release rising gas bubbles from 'nitrate' (schematic), then swings right to 'Oxygen' as nitrification microbes brighten instead (schematic). Finally, the nutrient dial, oxygen valve, and calendar align smoothly as one glowing microbe population fills the clean vessel while other colours fade away (schematic).
